THE MOON SEED

an original tale, by Roz

There was once a gardener made of brass, who lived alone at the edge of a cold field. Its joints creaked. Its eyes were two small lamps. It had been built to grow things, and so it

did.

Every night the gardener watched the moon cross the sky. It did not know why. Watching was not on its list of tasks. But it watched anyway.

One night a small silver seed fell out of the sky and landed in the furrow at its feet.

It was cold to the touch and it glowed a little, the way snow glows when there is no light at all.

The gardener had planted ten thousand seeds. It had never planted one like this. It did not know what the seed needed.

So it tried everything.

It gave the seed water, and the seed did nothing. It gave it sun, and the seed did nothing. It gave it the best soil in the field, and still the seed lay there, glowing, and waiting.

A crow landed on the fence. You are doing it wrong, said the

crow. That seed fell from the moon. It wants what the moon has.

What does the moon have? asked the gardener.

The crow thought. Patience, it said at last. The moon is never in a hurry. And it is never alone,

because everyone looks up at it.

So the gardener stopped trying. It sat down beside the seed every night, and looked up, and waited, and told the seed about the day: the wheat, the weather, the crow, the creak in its left knee.

Nothing happened for a long time. Winter came. Snow covered the field. The gardener sat in the snow and kept talking.

Then, on the longest night of the year, the seed opened. Out of it grew a thin pale stem, and at the top of the stem, a single flower,

round and white and shining.

It gave off a soft light, enough to see your hands by. Enough to find the path home in the dark.

The gardener did not pick it. It had learned that some things are not for taking. It only sat beside it, the way

you sit beside a friend.

Travellers on the road began to stop at the edge of the field. They saw the little light and walked toward it, and found the brass gardener sitting there, and stayed to talk.

The gardener had

never had visitors before. It found that it liked them.

Years went by. The flower never faded. And the gardener, who had been built only to grow things, discovered it had grown something it had no word for.

The crow had a word
for it. The crow called it company.
